title.raw: When to Go to the ER for High Blood Pressure: The 180/120 Rule
title.rendered: When to Go to the ER for High Blood Pressure: The 180/120 Rule

content.raw:
If your blood pressure is 180/120 or higher and you have symptoms, call 911. Those symptoms include a sudden severe headache, chest pain, trouble breathing, numbness, vision changes, or trouble speaking. If the reading is that high but you feel fine, wait 5 minutes and check again. If it is still high, call your healthcare provider the same day. This guide explains the 180/120 rule, which symptoms matter, and what happens at the ER.

What Blood Pressure Is Dangerously High?

A reading of 180/120 or higher is a hypertensive crisis. According to Cleveland Clinic, the top number can be 180 or higher, the bottom number can be 120 or higher, or both. Normal blood pressure is below 120/80.

Only one number has to cross the line. A reading of 182/95 counts, and so does 150/122.

Cleveland Clinic reports that about 1 to 2 out of every 100 people with high blood pressure have a hypertensive crisis. It can also happen to people who have never had blood pressure problems before.

High Reading With Symptoms: Call 911

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) says to call 911 if your reading is still high on a second check and you have any of these symptoms:

  • A sudden, severe headache
  • Difficulty breathing
  • Sudden, severe pain in your abdomen, chest, or back
  • Numbness or weakness
  • A sudden change in vision
  • Problems talking

The NHLBI is direct about the next step: do not wait to see if your pressure comes down on its own. These symptoms can mean the pressure is already damaging your heart, brain, or kidneys.

Several of these symptoms overlap with a stroke or heart attack. See our guides to recognizing a stroke and heart attack care.

High Reading, No Symptoms: Recheck First

A single high number on a home cuff does not always mean a crisis. The NHLBI gives a clear order of steps when you feel fine:

  1. Wait 5 minutes and check your blood pressure again.
  2. If it is still 180/120 or higher, call your healthcare provider. They may start a medicine or change your dose.
  3. If symptoms appear at any point, call 911.

Home readings are only useful if you know what to do with them. That is why physicians urge patients to agree on a plan ahead of time.

"If your blood pressure was much higher than usual and you have symptoms, your doctor might want you to call right away to discuss, or have you go to an emergency room, but if it's only slightly higher than usual your doctor might want you to recheck it again after five minutes, or even the next day."

Michael Rakotz, MD, family physician and group vice president of health outcomes at the AMA, in What doctors want patients to know about home BP measurement

What to Do at Each Reading

Your reading How you feel What to do
180/120 or higher Headache, chest pain, trouble breathing, numbness, vision change, or trouble speaking Call 911
180/120 or higher No symptoms Wait 5 minutes and recheck. If still high, call your provider the same day.
Below 180/120 but above your usual No symptoms Follow the plan you made with your doctor
Any reading Chest pain, stroke signs, or trouble breathing Call 911. These symptoms are emergencies at any blood pressure.

Why Is a Hypertensive Crisis an Emergency?

Blood pressure this high puts heavy strain on your blood vessels and organs. Cleveland Clinic warns that without treatment, a hypertensive crisis can cause life-threatening problems with the heart, kidneys, or brain.

That is why the symptoms matter so much. A severe headache or trouble speaking can point to the brain. Chest pain or trouble breathing can point to the heart.

What Happens at the ER for High Blood Pressure?

At ER of Irving, the team rechecks your blood pressure and asks about your symptoms and medicines. An EKG checks your heart, and our lab tests your blood and kidney function on site.

If a stroke or other brain problem is a concern, a CT scan is available on site at any hour. The physician then treats your blood pressure and anything the tests uncover. Learn more about our chest pain evaluation and stroke care.

We are open 24 hours a day at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX. Walk in any time, or call (972) 893-3148. If you have symptoms with a high reading, call 911 first.

FAQs

Is 180/110 an emergency?

Yes, it can be. The top number alone meets the crisis threshold of 180. If you have symptoms, call 911. If you feel fine, recheck after 5 minutes and call your provider if it stays high.

Should I go to the ER for blood pressure of 160/100?

A reading of 160/100 is high, but it is below the crisis threshold. Call your doctor soon to talk about it. Go to the ER if you have chest pain, stroke signs, or trouble breathing at any reading.

Should I drive myself to the ER with high blood pressure?

No, not if you have symptoms. The NHLBI advises calling 911. Paramedics can start care on the way, and you avoid driving while your brain or heart may be affected.

Can a headache mean my blood pressure is too high?

A sudden, severe headache with a reading of 180/120 or higher is an emergency. A sudden headache that feels like the worst of your life needs the ER at any reading. Read more in our guide to the worst headache of your life.

Should I go to the ER or urgent care for high blood pressure?

High blood pressure with symptoms belongs in the ER, where imaging and lab work are available at any hour. Our guide on ER vs. urgent care covers other conditions too.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: September 2026

title.raw: When to Go to the ER for the Flu: Warning Signs in Adults
title.rendered: When to Go to the ER for the Flu: Warning Signs in Adults

content.raw:
Most adults with the flu get better at home with rest and fluids. Go to the ER if you have trouble breathing, chest pain or pressure, or a seizure. Confusion or dizziness that will not go away, or no urination, also needs the ER. A fever or cough that improves and then comes back worse also needs emergency care. This guide covers each warning sign, who is at higher risk, and when to call 911 instead of driving.

Most Flu Does Not Need the ER

The flu makes you feel terrible, but feeling terrible is not the same as being in danger. The American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) notes that flu can often be managed at home with rest, fluids, and over-the-counter medicine.

The ER is for the minority of cases where the virus causes complications. Those complications can be serious, which is why the warning signs below matter.

"Emergency physicians routinely manage patients with severe flu, which can lead to complications and hospitalization."

L. Anthony Cirillo, MD, FACEP, president of ACEP, in an October 2025 ACEP statement

Flu Emergency Warning Signs in Adults

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists these emergency warning signs of flu in adults. If you have any of them, go to the ER:

  • Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath. Our breathing emergency team checks oxygen levels right away.
  • Persistent pain or pressure in the chest or abdomen.
  • Persistent dizziness, confusion, or trouble waking up.
  • Seizures.
  • Not urinating. This is a sign of serious dehydration.
  • Severe muscle pain.
  • Severe weakness or unsteadiness.
  • Fever or cough that improve but then return or worsen.
  • Worsening of a chronic medical condition, such as asthma, diabetes, or heart disease.

MedlinePlus adds a simple rule: any breathing problem with the flu is an emergency. Seek help right away.

When to Call 911 Instead of Driving

Call 911 if the person is struggling to breathe, has a seizure, cannot be woken, or has chest pain with sweating or nausea. Paramedics can start treatment on the way.

Do not drive yourself if you feel confused or faint. Ask someone else to drive, or call 911.

The Warning Sign People Miss: Better, Then Worse

A common pattern goes like this. The fever breaks, you start to feel human again, and then two days later the fever and cough come roaring back. Many people assume it is the same flu dragging on.

The CDC lists this pattern as an emergency warning sign. A relapse can mean a complication has set in. MedlinePlus lists pneumonia among the complications of flu, along with inflammation of the heart muscle and infections of the brain.

The flu can also strain the heart. During the severe 2017 to 2018 season, ACEP's president noted more irregular heart rhythms and heart attacks during or soon after the flu.

"If you have emergency warning signs or complications, go to the nearest emergency department immediately."

Paul Kivela, MD, MBA, FACEP, then president of ACEP, in ACEP's 2018 flu guidance

Who Is at Higher Risk of Flu Complications?

According to the CDC, some people are more likely to develop serious flu complications:

  • Adults 65 and older
  • People of any age with chronic conditions such as asthma, diabetes, or heart disease
  • Pregnant women
  • Children younger than 5, especially those younger than 2

If you are in one of these groups, MedlinePlus advises contacting your provider when you get the flu, even before any warning sign appears. For children, see our RSV vs. flu guide for parents.

What Should You Do at Home If You Have No Warning Signs?

If none of the warning signs apply, home care is usually the right call:

  • Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
  • Use fever reducers as the label directs.
  • Stay home and away from others, including people in your household, as much as you can.
  • Keep watching for the warning signs above.

MedlinePlus also advises contacting your provider if flu symptoms are very bad and not getting better. For adults, it advises calling right away for a fever that stays at or keeps rising above 103°F (39.4°C).

What Happens at the ER for the Flu?

At ER of Irving, an emergency physician checks your breathing, oxygen level, and hydration first. Our on-site lab runs flu and COVID testing, so you learn what you have during the same visit.

If pneumonia is a concern, a chest X-ray is taken on site. If you are dehydrated, IV fluids can start while you wait for results. The physician then recommends treatment based on what the tests show.

We are open 24 hours a day at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX. Walk in any time, or call (972) 893-3148. For severe breathing trouble or a seizure, call 911 first.

FAQs

Should I go to the ER or urgent care for the flu?

Mild flu without warning signs can be seen by your doctor or urgent care during open hours. Any emergency warning sign, such as trouble breathing or chest pain, belongs in the ER. Our guide on ER vs. urgent care walks through the choice condition by condition.

Is a high fever with the flu an emergency?

A high fever alone is common with flu. For adults, MedlinePlus advises calling your provider right away for a fever that stays at or rises above 103°F. The same goes for a fever lasting longer than 48 to 72 hours. Fever with confusion, a stiff neck, or trouble breathing needs the ER.

Can the ER test for the flu?

Yes. ER of Irving runs flu and COVID tests in our on-site lab at any hour. Results come back during your visit, so the physician can treat what you actually have.

When should a child with the flu go to the ER?

In children, the CDC warning signs include fast or labored breathing, bluish lips or face, and ribs pulling in with each breath. No urine for 8 hours is another. Any fever in a baby younger than 12 weeks also needs care. Our pediatric emergency team sees children 24 hours a day.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: September 2026

title.raw: When to Go to the ER for Vomiting and Diarrhea in Adults
title.rendered: When to Go to the ER for Vomiting and Diarrhea in Adults

content.raw:
Most vomiting and diarrhea from a stomach bug clears up on its own in a day or two. Go to the ER if you see blood or coffee-ground material in your vomit, or you have severe belly pain. Also go if you cannot keep fluids down for 12 hours or have not urinated in 8 hours. Black or bloody stools also need care right away. This guide covers every warning sign, how to spot dehydration, and what you can safely do at home.

Most Stomach Bugs Pass on Their Own

A sudden bout of vomiting and diarrhea is usually a viral stomach bug such as norovirus. It feels awful, but most healthy adults recover at home.

The simplest test is whether you can keep enough fluid down to keep urinating. Physicians use that same test.

"Norovirus can last for 24–48 hours. And if you can keep fluids down enough that you can urinate, you can most likely stay at home and let it run its course."

Joanna Turner Bisgrove, MD, family physician at Rush University Medical Center, in What doctors want patients to know about norovirus

Vomiting: When to Go to the ER

According to MedlinePlus, call 911 or go to the ER right away if:

  • You see blood or dark, coffee-colored material in the vomit.
  • You think the vomiting is from poisoning.

MedlinePlus also advises getting medical care right away if you have:

  • Vomiting for longer than 24 hours
  • Not been able to keep any fluids down for 12 hours or more
  • Not urinated for 8 hours or more
  • Severe stomach or belly pain
  • A headache or stiff neck
  • Vomited 3 or more times in 1 day

Diarrhea: When to Get Care Right Away

For diarrhea, MedlinePlus advises contacting a provider right away for:

  • Blood or pus in your stools
  • Black stools
  • Stomach pain that does not go away after a bowel movement
  • Diarrhea with a fever above 101°F (38.33°C)
  • Diarrhea that started after recent travel to a foreign country
  • Any signs of dehydration

Diarrhea that gets worse, or does not get better after 5 days in an adult, also needs a provider visit. If a provider is not available, the ER is open at any hour.

Signs of Dehydration in Adults

Dehydration is the main danger of vomiting and diarrhea. Watch for these signs, drawn from MedlinePlus:

  • Urinating less often, or dark yellow urine
  • Dizziness or lightheadedness
  • Dry mouth and increased thirst
  • Sunken eyes
  • Skin that does not bounce back when you pinch it

Dizziness when you stand, confusion, or no urine for 8 hours means dehydration is getting serious. Our guide to the signs of dehydration covers each one in detail.

"The key thing is hydration. The diarrhea and the vomiting can cause patients who are infected to lose body fluids."

Robyn F. Chatman, MD, MPH, family physician in Cincinnati, in What doctors want patients to know about norovirus

What Can You Do at Home?

If you have no warning signs, focus on replacing fluids:

  • Sip small amounts often. Large gulps can bring the vomiting back.
  • Choose drinks with electrolytes. In the AMA interview above, Dr. Chatman recommends non-carbonated electrolyte drinks with no citric acid for mild dehydration.
  • Skip caffeine. Dr. Chatman advises against it.
  • Avoid cold and flu medicine. She notes it can make you more dehydrated and does not treat a stomach bug.

Keep watching your urine. If it stops, or you cannot keep even small sips down, it is time to get care.

Could It Be Something Other Than a Stomach Bug?

Vomiting and diarrhea usually come from a virus, but not always. Food poisoning can cause the same symptoms, often within hours of a meal.

Belly pain that becomes severe or settles in one spot needs evaluation. Pain that moves to the lower right side can be a sign of appendicitis, which needs emergency care.

What Happens at the ER for Vomiting and Diarrhea?

At ER of Irving, an emergency physician checks how dehydrated you are and looks for a cause. Our on-site lab can check your electrolytes and kidney function during the visit.

If you are dehydrated, IV fluids replace what you have lost faster than drinking can. Imaging is available on site if the physician suspects something like appendicitis.

We are open 24 hours a day at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX. Walk in any time, or call (972) 893-3148. If there is blood in the vomit or you suspect poisoning, call 911.

FAQs

How long is too long to be throwing up?

MedlinePlus advises getting care if vomiting lasts longer than 24 hours. Get care sooner if you cannot keep fluids down for 12 hours or have not urinated in 8 hours.

Should I go to the ER for vomiting blood?

Yes. Blood or dark, coffee-colored material in the vomit means you should call 911 or go to the ER right away, according to MedlinePlus.

Is diarrhea for 3 days an emergency?

Not by itself. MedlinePlus advises seeing a provider if adult diarrhea does not get better after 5 days. Blood, black stools, a fever above 101°F, or signs of dehydration need care right away at any point.

Can the ER give IV fluids for dehydration?

Yes. IV fluids are one of the most common treatments for dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea. Read more in our guide to IV fluids for dehydration.

When should a child with vomiting go to the ER?

Children dehydrate faster than adults. See our guide to a baby or child who cannot keep liquids down for age-specific warning signs.

Should I go to the ER or urgent care for vomiting and diarrhea?

Mild symptoms without warning signs can be seen at urgent care during open hours. Blood, severe pain, or signs of serious dehydration belong in the ER. Our guide on ER vs. urgent care compares both.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: September 2026

FAQs

How long is too long to be throwing up?

MedlinePlus advises getting care if vomiting lasts longer than 24 hours. Get care sooner if you cannot keep fluids down for 12 hours or have not urinated in 8 hours.

Should I go to the ER for vomiting blood?

Yes. Blood or dark, coffee-colored material in the vomit means you should call 911 or go to the ER right away, according to MedlinePlus.

Is diarrhea for 3 days an emergency?

Not by itself. MedlinePlus advises seeing a provider if adult diarrhea does not get better after 5 days. Blood, black stools, a fever above 101°F, or signs of dehydration need care right away at any point.

Can the ER give IV fluids for dehydration?

Yes. IV fluids are one of the most common treatments for dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea. Read more in our guide to IV fluids for dehydration.

When should a child with vomiting go to the ER?

Children dehydrate faster than adults. See our guide to a baby or child who cannot keep liquids down for age-specific warning signs.

Should I go to the ER or urgent care for vomiting and diarrhea?

Mild symptoms without warning signs can be seen at urgent care during open hours. Blood, severe pain, or signs of serious dehydration belong in the ER. Our guide on ER vs. urgent care compares both.
